title: How are people using "mortified" wrongly? | EMOTION ETYMOLOGY

entries.note: Shares roots with [[same-root:satisfying]] and [[same-root:satiated]] and once meant full; someone sad has had enough, unlike Germanic cognates still meaning full.
Shares its root with [[same-root:sad]], from the Latin root meaning full.
Shares its root with [[same-root:sad]], from the Latin root meaning full.
Still means mood; humorism held that four bodily fluids, supposedly seen when blood separated, governed emotion and illness, with imbalances causing states like [[see:melancholy]].
Literally black bile, the humour whose excess caused sadness; the chol- part matches [[same-root:choleric]] and [[same-root:cholera]], the melan- part [[same-root:melanin]].
The dark pigment in skin, sharing the melan- element meaning black with [[same-root:melancholy]].
Describes the humoral state caused by an excess of yellow bile, sharing its chol- syllable with [[same-root:melancholy]].
Related to [[same-root:choleric]] because the disease was thought to be caused by an excess of bile.
Literally bloody, from French [[from:sang]], blood; too much blood was thought to cause an elevated, blissful mood, so the word is positive.
The fourth humour; its PH and silent G were added around the 1500s to show off its Greek roots, replacing an older, more sensible spelling.
Jess says too much [[from:phlegm]] supposedly made you angry, perhaps linked to foaming at the mouth, and was associated with heat.
Means under shade or shadow, related to [[same-root:umbra]], [[same-root:umber]] and [[same-root:umbrella]]; French sombre means dark.
Related to [[same-root:somber]] through the idea of shade.
Related to [[same-root:somber]] through the idea of shade.
Related to [[same-root:somber]] through the idea of shade.
Jess says it literally means full of memory, lingering sorrowfully on the past.
From Latin [[from:miserari]], to view with compassion, so originally pitiable, describing how others see you; related to [[same-root:miser]].
Related to [[same-root:miserable]]; originally someone to pity, it came to mean a wealthy person who spends like a poor one, like [[see:Scrooge]].
Probably from horses whose heavy neck crest flops to the side, though possibly from roosters, since it was paired with [[see:crest risen]] in the 1500s.
Paired with [[see:crestfallen]] in the 1500s and clearly referring to a rooster's crest.
From Middle English [[from:begon]], surrounded or overwhelmed, so beset by woe; Jess associates it with [[see:A Prairie Home Companion]].
Public radio series Jess associates with the word [[see:woebegone]], unsure if it is still on air.
Probably from [[from?:dull]] with the ending of [[see:tantrum]]; the hosts argue the calm sea region took its name from the word, not vice versa.
Probably the source of [[gave?:doldrums]].
Shares the ending that [[see:doldrums]] seems to have taken on.
Belt near the equator where ships get becalmed, which [[see:doldrums]] now typically refers to.
From Middle English [[from:dole]], grief, sorrow or mourning; Jess used to confuse it with [[see:baleful]].
Means wicked and cruel, from the Old English [[from:bale]], harm or evil, despite sounding like a sad howling dog.
An Old English kenning for a bringer of misfortune, built on [[from:bale]].
The go-to Old English negative emotion word, meaning harm or evil, now surviving only in [[gave:baleful]].
Early uses referred to animals, mostly rabid dogs; the anger and insanity senses share irrationality. It replaced [[see:wood]] and largely replaced [[see:wroth]].
The old go-to word for irrational behaviour, spelled w-o-d, replaced by [[see:mad]]; wood dogs were rabid dogs.
Once the common word for anger, largely replaced by [[see:mad]]; etymologically the same as [[same-root:wrath]], once written with two thorns.
The hosts work through their names, drawn from French and Germanic sources: [[see:wrath]], [[see:envy]], [[see:lust]], [[see:sloth]], [[see:pride]], [[see:greed]] and [[see:gluttony]].
Same word as [[same-root:wroth]]; the Old English form had one or two thorns, and the doubled consonant changed the vowel, yielding the two forms.
Old English letter looking like a P and B on top of one another, doubled in the Old English form of [[see:wrath]].
Old English letter like a D with a line through it, an alternative to [[see:thorn]] in spelling [[see:wrath]].
Noun-forming suffix, possibly the doubled thorn in [[see:wrath]], seen in [[see:growth]], [[see:strength]] and [[see:truth]].
Paired with [[see:growth]] as an example of the [[see:-th]] suffix.
Formed from [[from:grow]] with the [[see:-th]] suffix.
Paired with [[see:strength]] as an example of the [[see:-th]] suffix.
Formed from [[from:strong]] with the [[see:-th]] suffix.
Paired with [[see:truth]] as an example of the [[see:-th]] suffix.
Formed from [[from:true]] with the [[see:-th]] suffix.
Related to French [[same-root:envie]], from Latin [[from:invidere]], to look upon, implying maliciously; the vid- element appears in [[same-root:video]].
French word for a mild desire or feeling like something, related to [[same-root:envy]]; German [[equivalent:lust]] is its near-perfect equivalent.
Contains the Latin root for looking also behind [[same-root:envy]].
Spelled identically across Germanic languages; German Lust is mild desire, like having Lust for cake, and only English made it strongly sexual.
Cited as a less sexual, more warlike use of [[see:lust]].
Cited as a non-sexual use of [[see:lust]].
Corresponds to [[from:slow]] with the -th ending; the animal is named for its slowness, and it is etymologically the same word as [[same-root:sleuth (sloth)]].
The adjective that [[gave:sloth]] corresponds to.
Etymologically the same word as [[same-root:sloth]], surviving in the collective noun [[see:sleuth of bears]].
Discussed in an earlier Words Unravelled episode.
Essentially a sloth or laziness of bears, referring to their slow ambling and sleeping; uses [[see:sleuth (sloth)]] in its sloth sense.
The detective sense is a different, unrelated word from [[unrelated:sloth]], coming from [[from:sleuth hound]].
A kind of bloodhound good at following a trail, which gave the detective sense of [[gave:sleuth]].
Relates to [[same-root:proud]] by a vowel change, like [[see:fill]] and [[see:full]]; thought to come from a Latin word meaning it is useful; became sinful through church emphasis on humility.
Originally a positive word meaning magnificent; in manuals, something proud sticks out, literally [[see:outstanding]]; related to [[same-root:pride]].
Paired with [[see:full]] as a vowel-change parallel to [[see:pride]] and [[see:proud]].
Paired with [[see:fill]] as a vowel-change parallel to [[see:pride]] and [[see:proud]].
Paired with [[see:hale]] as a vowel-change parallel to [[see:pride]] and [[see:proud]].
Paired with [[see:heal]] as a vowel-change parallel to [[see:pride]] and [[see:proud]].
A figurative version of literally standing out, like something [[see:proud]] sticking out.
Like [[same-root:humiliated]] it literally means on the ground; the hosts mock people posting that they are humbled by awards.
Like [[same-root:humble]], literally means on the ground.
Means embarrassed, as in wanting to die; language creators say people misuse it to mean angry or upset, which Jess then saw in a video.
Reportedly often misused to mean amused, though Rob has never come across it.
A versatile prefix Jess has a video on; it can imbue something, as in [[see:bereaved]], or be privative, as in [[see:behead]].
Built with [[see:be-]], it implies something has been violently taken away, heavier than it sounds.
Example of [[see:be-]] used privatively, taking a head away rather than endowing one.
Old English word that already meant desirous or eager; the church condemned it, sometimes used synonymously with [[see:gluttony]].
From a Latin word meaning to gulp down, specifically eating too much, a sin for an age of food scarcity; unrelated to [[unrelated:gluten]].
Not related to [[unrelated:gluttony]].
Literally left with your mouth gaping open; the bash means to gape, the same as in [[same-root:bashful]].
Means shy, containing the same bash as [[same-root:abashed]], with a suffix instead of a prefix.
Via French, literally to be thundered at; the -ton- is the Latin word for thunder.
Its root means to flow, implying agitated water.
The feeling of something coming back to bite you, from Latin [[from:mordere]], to bite; [[same-root:morsel]] is related.
Related to [[same-root:remorse]] through the Latin for bite, a bite-sized piece.
Comes from [[from:bite]], going from a mouthful to any small portion, paralleling [[see:morsel]].
Sheep were thought unintelligent and easily deceived, so the sheepish have been deceived and are embarrassed; Rob jokes it's because they're baa-shful.
French emotion term from [[see:Susie Dent]]'s book, describing an extreme state.
The perfect retort you think of too late, on the staircase out; German [[equivalent:Treppenwitz]] is the same idea.
German term for thinking of the perfect comeback too late, equivalent to French [[equivalent:l'esprit de l'escalier]].
Japanese term for the misery of having had a bad haircut, which Rob feels often.
German emotion word cited as an example of Germany's fame for words for emotions English lacks.
German word for feeling shame on behalf of someone else.
Folk etymology reshaped [[from:shamefast]] as shame became negative, so it was misread as having shame all over your face.
Meant steadfast in modesty, a good thing, from an Old English predecessor; it became [[gave:shamefaced]].
Old English term for the genitals, something to be covered, like Latin [[equivalent:pudenda]].
Latin words pudenda or pudendum for the genitals, literally meaning shame limb, like Old English [[equivalent:shame limb]].
Middle English awk, turned the wrong way, plus the -ward of [[see:forward]]; originally an adverb meaning in the wrong direction, later socially backward.
Shares the -ward ending of [[see:awkward]].
Shares the -ward ending of [[see:awkward]].
Shares the -ward ending of [[see:awkward]].
Shares the -ward ending of [[see:awkward]].
Old English word meaning a guardian, the same word as [[same-root:guardian]] and [[same-root:warden]]; it forms part of [[gave:Edward]].
Exactly the same word as [[same-root:warden]] and [[same-root:ward]], borrowed from Parisian rather than Norman French.
Exactly the same word as [[same-root:guardian]], borrowed from Norman rather than Parisian French.
Name built from [[from:ward]], warden, and Old English [[from:ead]], happy, so happy warden, though ead also meant wealthy.
Meant both happy and wealthy, reflecting a Germanic link between wealth, luck and happiness; found in [[gave:Edward]] and [[gave:Edgar]].
Name from [[from:ead]], happy or wealthy, plus gar, spear, so happy spear.
Literally a ward for robes, protecting them; etymologically the same as [[same-root:garderobe]], borrowed from different French dialects.
Same word as [[same-root:wardrobe]], with the guard- form from Parisian rather than Norman French.
Rob's term for his mistaken parsing of [[see:painstaking]].
Rob confesses he said it as painstaking rather than pains-taking most of his life, until his [[see:eggcorn]] video.
Subject of a video Rob made about a year earlier.
Literally hair-raising, the hair bristling on your neck; structurally like [[see:terror]] via Old French and Latin but from a different root.
Means to tremble, from a different root than [[unrelated:horror]] despite the matching shape and French-style ending.
Still inspires horror, unlike [[see:terrific]], which has undergone amelioration.
Meant terrifying in the 1660s but now means great, a striking example of [[see:amelioration]], like [[see:awesome]].
Unlike [[see:terrific]], it still means horrible.
The process by which [[see:terrific]] went from terrifying to great.
Another example of amelioration like [[see:terrific]].
A very Victorian-seeming positive word compared with [[see:terrific]].
Past participle of [[from:affray]], meaning to frighten, merged with Old English [[from:afeared]].
Originally meant to frighten, now mostly legal; its past participle gave [[gave:afraid]].
From Greek [[from:hystera]], womb, so sexist; 1800s diagnoses listed wild symptoms used to institutionalise women; linked to the [[see:wandering womb]] theory.
Cited as one of the few remaining uses of [[see:hysteria]].
Ancient Greek medical theory blaming women's ailments on the uterus leaping around inside them, behind [[see:hysteria]].
Related to [[same-root:motion]] and [[same-root:move]], essentially motion with an e- prefix, so being moved.
Contained within, and related to, [[same-root:emotion]].
Related to [[same-root:emotion]].
Means to disturb or move in the mind, not necessarily negatively; related to [[same-root:emotion]].
Origin somewhat unknown, possibly related to Latin [[same-root?:pollex]] and Russian [[same-root?:palec]]; originally literal touching, later sensing in the mind.
Possibly related to [[same-root?:feeling]].
Possibly related to [[same-root?:feeling]].
Japanese for pictogram, coincidentally resembling [[unrelated:emote]] and [[see:emoticon]], which perhaps helped it spread in English.
Looks like [[see:emoji]] but does not mean the same.
From [[from:hap]], Old English for luck; many languages use the same word for happy and lucky, like German [[equivalent:glücklich]].
Old English word for luck, surviving in [[gave:happenstance]], [[gave:haphazard]], [[gave:happen]] and [[gave:happy]].
Contains [[from:hap]], luck.
Contains [[from:hap]], luck.
Now very vague, but from [[from:hap]], originally meaning something occurring by chance.
Preserves the chance sense of [[see:happy]].
German for happy, which also means lucky, ending in [[see:-lich (German)]].
German ending, like Dutch -lijk, that is the word [[same-root:like]] and corresponds to English [[same-root:-ly]].
Contains the same ending as [[see:-lich (German)]] and is cognate with German [[same-root:fröhlich]].
German for full of joy or merry, cognate with [[same-root:frolic]].
The same as German [[same-root:-lich (German)]] and English [[same-root:-ly]], and cognate with [[same-root:lich]], a body, implying similar form.
Adverb-forming ending; -ly words were originally like-words, matching German [[same-root:-lich (German)]] and Dutch and Scandinavian equivalents.
From an Old English word for a corpse, used for undead in fantasy games; cognate with [[same-root:like]], meaning body or form.
Danish and Norwegian word for happy that also means lucky, akin to [[equivalent:glücklich]].
Also standard Swedish for happy; from a root meaning to shine, related to [[same-root:yellow]], [[same-root:gold]], [[same-root:glow]] and [[same-root:glee]], with a past-participle ending.
Shares the Proto-Indo-European shine root with [[same-root:glad]].
Shares the Proto-Indo-European shine root with [[same-root:glad]].
Shares the shine root with [[same-root:glad]].
Shares the shine root with [[same-root:glad]].
Once spelled delite; its spelling was changed by analogy with [[unrelated:light]]; from a Latin word meaning to lure, like [[same-root:delicious]] and [[same-root:delectable]].
Influenced the spelling of [[unrelated:delight]], which has nothing to do with it.
From the same Latin luring root as [[same-root:delight]].
From the same Latin luring root as [[same-root:delight]].
